# Skales

> Websites & systems for service businesses. Builds websites, online booking and follow-up automation for UK service businesses (trades and local operators). Run by Tom Griffiths, one person, in the United Kingdom.

Key facts:
- Builds websites, online booking and follow-up automation for UK service businesses (trades and local operators).
- One person: the person you message is the person who builds it.
- Sixteen working demonstration builds run live on the site; every business in them is fictional.
- One system a week is built in public on Instagram.
- Clients own their domain, code and accounts from day one; nothing is rented back to them monthly.
- Every build is hand-coded with no page-builder, no theme and no third-party runtime dependencies.
- Contact: thomasrgriffiths08@gmail.com · Instagram @tomxsystems (https://www.instagram.com/tomxsystems/)
- Book a call: https://skales.com/book/

## Pages
- [Home](https://skales.com/): what Skales builds, with a live demonstration build on the page.
- [Work — sixteen builds](https://skales.com/work/): every demonstration build, each running live and each with its own page.
- [What I do](https://skales.com/what-i-do/): the three services — capture websites, online booking with a pipeline, missed-call and review automation — with the systems running, and the four-step process.
- [Why](https://skales.com/why/): ownership (clients own domain, code and accounts), one person, built in public, and the FAQ.
- [Book a call](https://skales.com/book/): four qualifying questions, then a slot straight into the diary.
- [Free teardown](https://skales.com/teardown.html): three details in, three findings back by message.
- [Notes](https://skales.com/notes/): short pieces — what a missed call actually costs a service business; why i don’t rent you your own website; sixteen builds for businesses that don’t exist, on purpose.

## The sixteen builds
- [Northgate Quote Engine](https://skales.com/work/northgate-quote-engine/): business tool for an invented kitchen fitter — A quote that assembles itself while the customer answers.
- [Redgate Job & Lead System](https://skales.com/work/redgate-job-system/): business tool for an invented heating & plumbing — Every enquiry, where it came from, and what happened to it.
- [Halcyon Dispatch](https://skales.com/work/halcyon-dispatch/): business tool for an invented heating dispatch team — Drag a job to another engineer and the week re-plans itself.
- [Ledgerline](https://skales.com/work/ledgerline/): business tool for an invented invoice & proposal studio — A live A4 page that reflows as you type.
- [Mortgage Lab](https://skales.com/work/mortgage-lab/): business tool for an invented broker lead magnet — What an overpayment really saves, month by month.
- [Payslip Lab](https://skales.com/work/payslip-lab/): business tool for an invented accountant lead magnet — Gross to net, and the 60% trap nobody explains.
- [Kerbside Scorecard](https://skales.com/work/kerbside-scorecard/): business tool for an invented google profile report card — Marks a Google Business Profile like an exam.
- [Stopcock](https://skales.com/work/stopcock/): business tool for an invented missed-call leak meter — What unanswered calls cost you a year.
- [Turnover](https://skales.com/work/turnover/): business tool for an invented roofing firm rebuild — Drag the tape line across a 2011 site and its rebuild.
- [Fenwick Booking](https://skales.com/work/fenwick-booking/): business tool for an invented heating engineer — Service, slot, deposit, confirmed — no phone tag.
- [Jobsheet](https://skales.com/work/jobsheet/): business tool for an invented van-side job report — Fill it in from the van, the customer report writes itself.
- [Shiftbook](https://skales.com/work/shiftbook/): business tool for an invented salon staff rota — Click a cell to place a shift. Clashes flag as you go.
- [Atelier Voss](https://skales.com/work/atelier-voss/): website for an invented architecture practice — A studio site with no photographs at all.
- [Cadence](https://skales.com/work/cadence/): website for an invented field-ops software — The page is an operations board that never stops running.
- [MARÉE — Sel Obscur](https://skales.com/work/maree/): website for an invented fragrance house — Ink through water, and a page that darkens as you descend.
- [SIGNAL 2027](https://skales.com/work/signal/): website for an invented music & light festival — Type that reacts to how hard you scroll.

## Frequently asked
- **Do I actually own the website?** Yes. With Skales the domain, the code and the hosting sit in your own accounts from day one. It is set up so you could walk away tomorrow and lose nothing; that is the whole point.
- **Is there a monthly fee to keep my site online?** No. Skales does not charge a monthly platform fee to keep your own website alive. You pay for hosting and your domain directly, in your own name, at cost. If any quote you get includes a monthly fee to keep your own site online, that is rent.
- **How long does a build take?** A capture website takes days. A full system with booking and follow-up usually takes one to two weeks. You get a date with the quote, and you can watch it being built in public.
- **Are the sixteen builds on this site real clients?** No, and deliberately so. Every business, person, review and phone number in the demonstration builds is invented, so nothing on this site exposes anyone Skales works with. They are real working software, just for businesses that do not exist.
- **Who actually does the work?** Tom Griffiths. Skales is one person: there is no account manager and no handover to a junior. The person you message is the person who builds it.
- **What kind of businesses is this for?** UK service businesses whose work comes in by phone: plumbers, heating engineers, electricians, roofers, kitchen fitters, landscapers, cleaners, salons and similar trades and local operators.
- **What happens after I book a call or send the form?** Tom Griffiths looks at your website, your Google listing and what happens when someone tries to reach you, then messages you three things: what is leaking, what to fix first, and what it is worth in jobs. If you want it fixed, you get a flat quote. If not, you keep the list.
- **Do you use page-builders or templates?** No. Every build is hand-coded with no page-builder, no theme and no third-party runtime dependencies. Every visual is drawn in code rather than bought from a stock library.

### Own it. Don’t rent it. — https://skales.com/why/

Why — one person, built in public, you own it | Skales Skip to content s k ales --:--:-- UK standby Work 16 What I do Why Notes Book a call Work 16 What I do Why Notes Book a call Free teardown Why One person Built in public Own it. Don t rent it. Skales exists because most service businesses are renting their own website from whoever built it, and getting a brochure for the money. This page is the reasoning, and the straight answers. Ownership Yours from day one Why should you own your own website? You should own your website because it is where your work comes from, and anything that important should not depend on a monthly payment to the person who built it. With Skales, the domain, the code and every account sit in the client s name from the first day. Some builders charge every month, forever, just to keep a site alive. A page-builder account the site cannot leave, a domain registered in the agency s name, a platform fee each one is a lever, and it only gets pulled one way. Straight answers The questions people ask Questions people ask Skales Do I actually own the website? Yes. With Skales the domain, the code and the hosting sit in your own accounts from day one. No. Skales does not charge a monthly platform fee to keep your own website alive. You pay for hosting and your domain directly, in your own name, at cost. Tom Griffiths looks at your website, your Google listing and what happens when someone tries to reach you, then messages you three things: what is leaking, what to fix first, and what it is worth in jobs. ### What a missed call actually costs a service business — https://skales.com/notes/what-a-missed-call-costs/

What a missed call actually costs a service business Skip to content s k ales --:--:-- UK standby Work 16 What I do Why Notes Book a call Work 16 What I do Why Notes Book a call Free teardown Home / Notes 3 September 2026 Tom Griffiths What a missed call actually costs a service business The sum behind the missed-call text-back, with every assumption on the table — and why the number survives a sceptic. A missed call costs a service business more than the job on the other end of it, because the customer who rang is usually ringing the next firm on the list within the hour. The Stopcock calculator on this site meters that leak from five numbers you already know: calls per week, the share you miss, the value of an average job, how many quotes turn into work, and the share of missed callers who are gone for good. Why the model has a "gone for good" factor Most missed-call calculators quietly assume every missed caller would have booked. They would not. Some ring back, some were price-checking, some booked elsewhere before you saw the voicemail. Stopcock makes that share an explicit slider, so the headline figure is a floor a sceptical owner can defend, not a marketing number. What a text-back in under a minute changes A missed-call text-back sends the customer a message seconds after the ring-out, asks one question, and turns a voicemail into a conversation. The customer who was about to dial the next number replies instead. The follow-up automation on this site does exactly that, and the Redgate demo on the Why page shows the sequence end to end. Open the calculator, put your own numbers in, and argue with it. That is what it is for. ### Why I don’t rent you your own website — https://skales.com/notes/why-i-dont-rent-you-your-own-website/

Here is what you own it actually means in practice. A website built by this studio belongs to the business it was built for: the domain, the code and every account sit in the client’s name from the first day. If the client walks away tomorrow, the site keeps working, because nothing about it depends on a monthly payment to the person who built it. What "rent" looks like A monthly platform fee to keep your own site online. A page-builder account the site cannot leave. A domain registered in the agency’s name. Each one is a lever, and the lever only ever gets pulled one way. What ownership looks like Hand-written code with no page-builder and no theme, hosted in an account the client controls, with the domain registered to the client. Every build on the Work page of this site was made that way, and every client build is made the same way. Why do it this way Because the work should be good enough that people stay by choice. Rent is what you charge when you are not sure it is. ### Sixteen builds for businesses that don’t exist, on purpose — https://skales.com/notes/sixteen-builds-all-fictional/

Sixteen builds for businesses that don’t exist, on purpose Skip to content s k ales --:--:-- UK standby Work 16 What I do Why Notes Book a call Work 16 What I do Why Notes Book a call Free teardown Home / Notes 3 September 2026 Tom Griffiths Sixteen builds for businesses that don’t exist, on purpose Why every demo on this site is for an invented company, and why that is better proof than a client logo wall. Every one of the sixteen builds on this site was made for a business that does not exist: Redgate Heating, Northgate Kitchens, Atelier Voss, Fenwick Heating and the rest are invented, and so is every person, review and phone number inside them. That is deliberate. It means nothing on this site exposes a real client’s numbers, customers or setup. Why fictional beats a logo wall A logo wall proves someone paid. A working build proves what was built. Each demo here runs live in the page: you can drag a job across the dispatch board, take a slot in the booking flow, or watch the quote engine price a kitchen. A screenshot of a client site cannot do that, and a client site should not be handed to strangers to click through. What a real build shares with these The approach is identical: hand-coded, no page-builder, no stock imagery, built to do one job for one kind of business, and owned outright by the client. The only difference is whose name is on it.
